entry.title: I built a SaaS landing page in a week to validate my idea — here's what I shipped and learned
entry.summary:
The Problem with Building First
I'm a developer. I love building things. But I've watched too many indie founders (myself included) spend Have idea Get excited Build product Launch to crickets Wonder what went wrong This time I tried something different: validate before building. A landing page for cos — an AI agent that handles the The angle that makes it different: it connects to your GitHub Live link: cos-landingpage.vercel.app I almost charged $29/mo. Then I remembered: solo founders are Final pricing: Solo: $19/mo (500 credits) Founder: $49/mo (2,000 credits) Team: $129/mo (6,000 credits) Waitlist gets 50% off first 3 months. After that, full price. Why credit-based instead of unlimited? Because LLM APIs cost Margin math: ~85% gross margin at 50 users using multi-model Posted to 3 subreddits last night before bed. Woke up to: 8 unique visitors 24 page views (3 pages per visitor — they're scrolling) 1 signup (12.5% conversion rate) 1 detailed feedback comment from a 3-year solo founder That feedback was worth more than 100 upvotes. They confirmed Today: Post to more communities (DEV.to obviously, HN tonight) This week: DM 10 founders directly for deeper feedback Day 14: Decide based on data: 30+ signups + meaningful feedback → build it 10-30 signups → iterate positioning <10 signups → kill it or pivot I'll post a follow-up either way. Transparency is the only If you're a solo founder sitting on an idea, scared to build Build a landing page. Ship it. Share it. See if anyone cares. Worst case: you waste a week instead of 6 months. If this resonates, I'd love your honest feedback on the cos-landingpage.vercel.app Roast it, point out positioning gaps, tell me if the pain Thanks for reading.

entry.title: Laravel Valet Certificate Showing on analytics.google.com? Root Cause and Fix
entry.summary:
Originally published at recca0120.github.io You open analytics.google.com in Chrome and click the certificate — and see this: Subject: filament-scu.test Issuer: Laravel Valet CA Self Signed CN
That's not Google's certificate. That's your local Laravel Valet CA leaking onto an external site. This isn't a browser bug or a Google problem — it's your local dev environment intercepting traffic it shouldn't. Valet builds a local dev stack out of three components: dnsmasq: resolves *.test domains to 127.0.0.1
nginx: listens on 127.0.0.1, routes requests to local sites by server_name
Valet CA: signs HTTPS certificates for each .test site In a correct setup, /etc/resolver/test scopes only *.test lookups to dnsmasq; external domains go through the system DNS. The two never cross paths. But ther…

entry.title: Why I Built TokenBar: AI Spend Should Not Be a Monthly Surprise
entry.summary: A lot of AI cost advice starts too late. It tells you to review the bill after the damage is done. That never worked for me. The real problem is not that AI is expensive. The problem is that the expensive part happens quietly. One more prompt. One more rewrite. One more huge context dump. Then you look up later and realize you spent money on a conversation that had stopped being useful. That is why I built TokenBar. TokenBar is a macOS menu bar app that keeps token usage and spend visible while I am actually working. Not in a dashboard. Not in a tab I will check later. Right there in the menu bar, where the number can bother me before the bill does. That tiny shift changed how I use AI: I notice runaway loops faster I stop pretending giant context windows are free I choose cheaper models when the task does not need the expensive one I catch waste while I can still do something about it I did not build TokenBar because I wanted another chart. If you are shipping with Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, or any other metered tool, the most useful thing you can do is make the cost visible while you work. That is the whole product.

entry.title: Introducing SQL Explorer: Direct SQL Access to Onchain Data
entry.summary: Trading desks and quant teams building on Hyperliquid spend weeks on data plumbing before they get to the query they actually care about. SQL Explorer replaces that stack with a single interface. No indexer. No pipelines. Just SQL.
